entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Concept
Inducement: a liquidity trap
After a sweep and a structure shift, price often pauses and leaves a small, tidy zone close to current price. It has a break of structure, a pullback and sometimes an imbalance. It looks like the entry. Its real job is to collect buyers and their stops, so that price has something to take on its way to the zone the move actually came from.
Drawn as longs
Concept, no pair named
Mirror for shorts
From the post's closing slide
“The first setup that looks valid is often not the best one. The better entry usually comes after the trap, not before it.”
1 · Two zones
2 · Why it looks clean
3 · Early entries stopped
4 · The real zone
Telling them apart
Entry, SL & TP
Repeatable steps
In the case studies
How to read this page
The slides show one candle chart at three moments, plus one line drawing of the same idea. No pair, timeframe or price scale is given. X marks a liquidity sweep. $$$ marks resting liquidity. BSL is buy-side liquidity. Where I give a reward-to-risk figure it is measured from the drawn boxes.

entries.h: One move, two zones
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. A range low is swept (X), a large bullish candle breaks structure (MSS), price pauses briefly and continues up. Two demand zones are marked: a lower one at the base of the large candle and an upper one at the pause, with a liquidity line under the upper one.
Slide 1 — “Inducement: A Liquidity Trap.”
Step 1 · The setup
One move, two zones
What the chart shows
A range, then a sweep (X). Price drifts sideways. A wick runs under the earlier low of the range and is rejected.
MSS on one large candle. A single bullish candle closes above the range high. This is the displacement.
The lower zone. Drawn at the base of that candle, where the move began. Price has not been back to it.
A short pause, then continuation. Two small candles pull back a little. The next candle breaks to a new high.
The upper zone. Drawn around that pause. The line under it is marked $$$: the low of the pause, where stops will sit.
The question the slide is asking
Both boxes are demand zones by the usual definition. The upper one is closer, it formed after the shift and it led to a new high. The lower one is further away and needs a deeper pullback. Which do you buy?
The label gives it away. The upper zone has liquidity marked directly beneath it. The lower one has nothing beneath it except the sweep that has already happened.
Rule to carry forward
When two zones are stacked, ask which one is the origin of the displacement that broke structure. That is the real zone. A zone formed after the break, on the way up, is a candidate for inducement.

entries.h: Why the trap looks like a clean entry
entries.t:
Chart: Line diagram. Price rallies from a higher-timeframe order block, breaks structure, and returns to a zone labelled Inducement where it sweeps a low and shifts up; a long is taken and then stopped out as price falls through the zone. Price then sweeps a low inside the higher-timeframe order block, shifts up, and a second long from a lower-timeframe order block reaches the target.
Slide 2 — “A small structure forms. A BOS, a pullback, maybe a IBM. It looks like a clean entry.”
Step 2 · The trap in detail
Why the trap looks like a clean entry
This drawing shows two trades with the same pattern. The first loses. The second wins. Read it left to right.
The first trade: at the inducement zone
Price leaves the HTF order block and breaks structure (BoS). The pullback low that led to the break is boxed and labelled Inducement, with $$$ under it.
Price returns to that zone.
Inside it, a small low is swept (X) and structure shifts up (MSS). That is a complete confirmation pattern.
A long is taken. The first position box: entry at the top of the zone, stop just under the $$$ low.
Price falls straight through. The $$$ low and the stop are taken.
The second trade: at the HTF order block
Price carries on down into the HTF OB.
The same pattern prints again. A low is swept (X), then an MSS.
A long is taken from the LTF order block that the shift leaves behind, with the stop under the sweep low.
Price rallies to the earlier high. About three times the risk on the drawing.
Why this matters
This is the uncomfortable part. The first trade was not careless. It waited for a sweep and a shift, which is exactly what the confirmation model asks for. It still lost, because of where it happened: above the higher-timeframe zone, with a clean low underneath it and the real zone still untouched below that.
Rule to carry forward
A confirmation pattern is only as good as its location. Sweep plus shift inside the higher-timeframe zone is a signal. The same pattern above the zone, with liquidity resting beneath it, is bait.
The slide text says “IBM”. From the other posts I read it as IMB, imbalance.

entries.h: Traders enter early and are stopped
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart continued. Price has made a new high and fallen back into the upper zone. A long position is drawn from the top of the upper zone with its stop under the liquidity line; the last candle's wick goes below that stop. An imbalance separates the upper and lower zones, and a BSL line marks the target above.
Slide 3 — “Traders enter early. Price goes against them and takes their stops.”
Step 3 · The trap closes
Traders enter early and are stopped
What happened
Price made its new high and turned. A run of bearish candles brings it back to the upper zone.
The early long. The position box shows the trade most people take: buy the top of the upper zone, stop just under the $$$ low, target the BSL line at the top.
Price stalls inside the zone. A few small candles. It looks like the zone is holding.
One candle drops through the $$$ line. Its wick goes below the stop. The early longs are out.
An imbalance lies below (IMB). The gap left by the displacement candle sits between the two zones and has not been filled.
What gave it away beforehand
An unfilled imbalance directly beneath the upper zone.
An untouched zone at the origin of the move, beneath the imbalance.
A single obvious low under the upper zone for stops to gather at.
A shallow pullback. The upper zone is roughly at the middle of the leg; the lower zone is in the discount half.
Rule to carry forward
Before buying a zone, look underneath it. If there is an unfilled imbalance and an untouched origin zone below, expect price to go there, and expect the stops under your zone to be taken on the way.

entries.h: Only then does price reach the real zone
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart continued. Price falls through the upper zone and the imbalance, a wick touches the top of the lower zone, and price then rallies up to and through the BSL line.
Slide 4 — “Only then does price reach the real zone. This is where the move starts.”
Step 4 · The real entry
Only then does price reach the real zone
What happened
Price kept falling after the stops were taken. It filled the imbalance.
A wick touched the top of the lower zone. Just the edge, then a close back above.
Price turned and rallied. Back up through the upper zone, to the earlier high, then on to the BSL line and through it.
The position box still on the slide is the early trade from slide 3, shown for comparison. Its target was reached in the end, but only after its stop had been hit.
What to take from it
The early traders had the direction and the target right. They lost on location alone.
The fill at the real zone was a wick. A limit order at the top edge filled. Waiting to watch a reaction would have meant chasing.
The trap supplied the fuel. Stops from the early longs are sell orders. They gave larger buyers something to fill against at a better price.
Rule to carry forward
Put the limit order at the origin zone and treat everything above it as liquidity. The better entry comes after the trap, not before it.

entries.h: Inducement or the real zone?
entries.t:
Telling them apart
Inducement or the real zone?
The slides show what inducement looks like after the fact. The table below turns that into checks you can run beforehand. The first two rows come from the slides. The rest are my reading.
| Check | Inducement | Real zone
| What is underneath it? | A clean low with stops ($$$), and often an unfilled imbalance | The sweep low. The liquidity there has already been taken
| How did it form? | A pause or small pullback after structure had already broken | The base of the displacement that broke structure
| Where is it in the leg? | Shallow, around or above the midpoint | Deep, in the discount half
| Where is it relative to the HTF zone? | Above it. Price has left the HTF zone and not come back | Inside it
| Is another untouched zone below? | Yes | No. It is the last zone before the sweep low
| How obvious is it? | Very. It is the first thing everyone sees | Less. It needs a deeper pullback that feels like the move is failing
The first zone sometimes holds
None of these checks is certain. In a strong trend price can turn at the shallow zone and never come back for the deep one. If you always wait for the origin zone you will miss those moves. That is the price of avoiding the trap, and it is why the post says “often” and “usually”, not “always”.

entries.h: Entry, stop loss and take profit
entries.t:
Order placement
Entry, stop loss and take profit
For the trade at the real zone. The candle slides do not draw this position, so the placements follow the line drawing on slide 2 and the case studies.
Entry
Buy limit at the top edge of the origin zone.
The origin zone is the base of the displacement candle that made the MSS.
On the candle chart only a wick reached it. A limit at the edge filled.
Stricter version, from the line drawing: wait for a sweep and MSS inside the zone and buy the LTF order block it leaves.
Stop loss
Below the origin zone, under the sweep low.
The sweep low (X) is where the whole move began. If it breaks, the idea is finished.
In the line drawing the stop sits at the low of the sweep inside the HTF OB.
Never under the inducement low. That is the level price is being drawn to.
Take profit
The high above, or the BSL beyond it.
The line drawing targets the high made before the pullback, at about 1:3.
The candle chart marks a BSL line higher up, which price also reached.
The entry is lower than the early trader's and the target is the same, so the deeper zone can pay more per unit of risk.

entries.h: Step-by-step for the next trade
entries.t:
Repeatable strategy
Step-by-step for the next trade
Written for longs. For shorts, mirror it.
Find the sweep and the shift.A low taken and rejected, then a displacement candle closing above the prior high.
Mark the origin zone.The base of the displacement candle, above the sweep low. Place the buy limit at its top edge.
Mark every zone and low that forms above it afterwards.Pauses, small pullbacks, first higher lows. Label each one as liquidity, not as an entry.
Check what lies between price and the origin zone.An unfilled imbalance or an untaken low means price has a reason to come down.
If price reacts at an upper zone, do nothing.Even if it prints a sweep and a shift there. Note the new low it leaves.
If price runs to target without you, accept it.Cancel the order. Record it as a missed trade.
When price reaches the origin zone, the order fills.Stop under the sweep low, target at the high above. At least 1:2, risk 0.5–1%.

entries.h: Where this has already appeared
entries.t:
In the case studies
Where this has already appeared
| Case | The inducement | What price did
| AUD/USD long | The IDM low after the shift, then a bounce above the zone that left a $$$ low | Took both, then filled deep in the M15 demand about 13 hours after the shift
| BTC/USD long | A sharp pullback that turned just above the order block, leaving a $$ low | Rallied to a new high, then came back through that low deep into the order block
| GBP/JPY long | A wick low and a cluster of lows sitting above the order block | Swept both, then one wick tapped the order block about 12 hours after the shift
| GBP/AUD long | The IDM low left just after the shift | Took it, filled the imbalance and touched the 15m demand about 3 hours after the shift
| USD/JPY long (1H) | Twice: the 30m pullback low before the BoS, then the 15m pullback low after the shift | Took the first on the way to the 30m demand and the second on the way to the 15m demand
| XAU/USD short (15m) | The internal high at 3,893.3 left above the supply entry | Never taken: price fell from a two-point tag of the zone edge and the X stayed above the trade the whole way
| XAU/USD short (4H→15m) | The $$$ internals left under the OB, between entry and SSL | Taken on the way down as part of the move; the fall ran through them to the SSL line
In six of the seven, the liquidity resting in front of the zone was taken first — for the 4H-to-15m gold short, the $$$ internals under the block went on the way down. The 15m gold supply short remains the exception: the high above the entry was never taken and the trade worked anyway. Log that as the exception it is, not as permission to short under untouched liquidity. The AUD/USD case is the closest match to this page: it uses the IDM label and nearly the same slide captions.
Compare this with the entry models. The confirmation entry asks for a sweep and a shift before entering. This page adds the condition that makes it work: the sweep and shift have to happen at the zone, not above it.
Keep this in proportion
Every example on this site was chosen because the deep zone was reached and held. To know how often that happens, you need the other outcomes too: the times the shallow zone held and the trade was missed, and the times the origin zone was reached and failed. Log all three when you backtest.
Open the playbookAll case studies

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Concept
Internal and external structure, and their sweeps
External structure is the main swings that set the trend. Internal structure is the smaller swings inside one of those legs. Each has its own liquidity and its own sweeps. Knowing which one you are looking at tells you whether a move is the trend changing, or only a pullback collecting orders on its way to your zone.
Drawn as a long
No pair named
Mirror it for shorts
Two structures
How to mark them
Two kinds of break
Two kinds of liquidity
The four sweeps
Internal to external
In the routine
Timeframes
Mistakes
Checklist

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Two structures on one chart
entries.t:
Part 1
Two structures on one chart
Filled dots are external swing points. Open dots are internal swing points.
External structure
The main swing highs and lows on the timeframe you are reading.
It decides the trend: higher highs and higher lows, or lower lows and lower highs.
A candle close beyond an external point is a real break of structure (BoS), or a change of direction if it is against the trend.
The protected low or high is always an external point.
Internal structure
The smaller highs and lows inside one external leg, mostly inside the pullback.
It shows how the pullback is developing and when it is ending.
A close beyond an internal point is an internal break. It is an early sign, not a trend change.
Internal highs and lows are where inducement forms.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: How to mark them the same way every time
entries.t:
Part 2
How to mark them the same way every time
The labels need one fixed rule, or you will redraw them to suit the trade you want.
Start from the last break of structure.Find the last candle close above an external high (uptrend).
Confirm the external low.The lowest point of the pullback before that break becomes the external higher low. A low is only confirmed as external once the high after it has been broken.
Mark the external high.The highest point reached after the break, once price starts pulling back.
Everything between them is internal.Every smaller high and low between the external low and the external high belongs to internal structure, however clear it looks.
Update only on a close.The external points move only when a candle closes beyond one of them. Wicks do not move them.
This is a judgement, so keep it simple
Traders draw internal and external structure slightly differently, and no version is the official one. What matters is that you use one rule, the same way, on every chart. The rule above is the one this site uses: a swing point is external when it caused, or was made by, a break of structure.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Two kinds of break
entries.t:
Part 3
Two kinds of break
| | Internal break | External break (BoS)
| What closes | A candle beyond a small high or low inside the leg | A candle beyond a main swing high or low
| What it means | The pullback is turning, or only pausing | The trend continues, or has changed
| Changes your direction? | No | Yes, if it is against the trend
| How you use it | As the shift for an entry, but only at a marked zone and after a sweep | To set long or short, the protected point and the target
Rule
An internal break against the external trend is a pullback until an external point breaks. Do not sell an uptrend because a small low gave way. That move is usually price coming down to your demand.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Two kinds of liquidity
entries.t:
Part 4
Two kinds of liquidity
| | Internal liquidity | External liquidity
| Where it sits | Inside the current range: under internal lows, above internal highs, at inducement points, and in unfilled imbalances and zones | Outside the current range: above the external high and below the external low; also previous day and week highs and lows, and clear equal highs or lows at the range edge
| Who is there | Early buyers and sellers with tight stops | Swing stops and breakout orders
| What price does with it | Takes it during the pullback, on the way to a zone | Travels to it after the zone holds. It is the target
For more on where stops collect, see liquidity and inducement.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: The four sweeps, and what each one tells you
entries.t:
Part 5
The four sweeps, and what each one tells you
A sweep is always the same event: price trades beyond a level, takes the stops and closes back. Where it happens decides what it means.
1
Internal sweep during the pullback
Price takes an internal low on the way down, before it has reached your zone. This is inducement being cleared.
Meaning: the pullback is still running.
Action: none. Keep waiting for the zone.
2
Internal sweep at the zone
Price takes an internal low inside or just into your demand, then turns.
Meaning: the pullback may be finishing here.
Action: wait for the shift, then place the order. The stop goes below this sweep.
3
External sweep with the trend
Price runs above the external high and takes the stops there.
Meaning: the target has been reached.
Action: the trade is over. A close above gives a new BoS; a wick only can start a deeper pullback.
4
External sweep against the trend
Price dips below the external low, closes back above it, and then shifts up.
Meaning: the largest pool of sell stops has been taken and the trend has held. This is the strongest sweep.
Action: trade it with the sweep model. If candles close below instead, it is a break and the trend has changed.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Price moves from internal liquidity to external liquidity
entries.t:
Part 6
Price moves from internal liquidity to external liquidity
After a break, price comes back inside the range to collect internal liquidity and fill a zone. Then it leaves for the external liquidity on the other side. Then the cycle repeats.
Pullback
Price works down through internal lows. Each one taken is an internal sweep. None of them is a reason to buy yet.
Zone
The last internal sweep happens at demand. The shift that follows is an internal break in the direction of the external trend.
Expansion
Price runs to the external high. That is where the trade is closed, because that is where the opposite orders are waiting.
Rule
Enter on internal liquidity being taken. Exit at external liquidity. If you are entering where external liquidity sits, you are probably the liquidity.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Where this fits in the routine
entries.t:
Part 7
Where this fits in the routine
These are the same steps as the trading notes, with the structure named.
| Note | Which structure | What to check
| 1 Trend | External, higher timeframe | A close beyond an external high or low. Internal breaks do not count.
| 2 Sweep before the break | Either | The pullback took a low before the high broke. An internal low taken is the minimum. A dip under the previous external low that closed back above is stronger.
| 3 Protected low | External | The low of that pullback. It is now the external higher low.
| 4 Demand | External leg | The zone at the origin of the leg that broke the external high.
| 5 Target | External liquidity | The external high, or the supply in front of it.
| 6 Return | Internal, higher timeframe | Internal lows are taken on the way down. Do nothing.
| 7 Sweep in the zone | Internal, lower timeframe | A lower-timeframe low is taken at the zone. The protected low has not been closed below.
| 8 Shift | Lower timeframe | A close above the last lower high. On the higher timeframe this is only an internal break, which is why it needs the zone and the sweep with it.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Internal on one timeframe is external on the next
entries.t:
Part 8
Internal on one timeframe is external on the next
The two words are relative to the chart you are on.
The internal structure of the 4H is roughly the external structure of the 15m.
So when the 15m breaks its own external high inside a 4H demand, the 4H sees only an internal break. Both are true.
Name the timeframe every time: “4H external high”, “15m external low”. It removes most of the confusion.
Take direction and target from the higher timeframe’s external structure. Take the entry from the lower timeframe’s structure. See top-down analysis.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Common mistakes
entries.t:
Common mistakes
Calling an internal break a trend change and trading against the external trend.
Buying the first internal sweep in the middle of the pullback, before price has reached a zone.
Putting the target at an internal high. Price can stall there, but the draw is the external high.
Putting the stop behind an internal low that has not been swept. It is liquidity, and the pullback is likely to take it.
Treating a close below the external low as a sweep. A sweep closes back inside; a close beyond is a break.
Re-labelling the external points after the fact so the trade looks valid.

entries.p: Internal and External Structure and Sweeps
entries.h: Checklist
entries.t:
Repeatable
Checklist
Where are the external high and low?Marked on the higher timeframe, from the last break of structure.
Which way did the last external break go?That is the only direction I trade.
Is the current move internal?Yes while price is between the two external points. I treat it as a pullback.
Where is the internal liquidity?Internal lows above my zone. I expect them to be taken first.
Has an internal sweep happened at my zone?Yes, with the protected low still intact. Now I wait for the shift.
Where is the external liquidity?Above the external high. That is the target.
What cancels it?A candle close below the external low.

entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Method · Key points

Everything the other pages teach, distilled to the lines that actually decide trades. Read it before the session. Then close it and mark your own chart — the point of this page is that you never need it open while you trade.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: The only sequence
entries.t:
The only sequence
Every trade on this site is the same six lines, in this order. Written for longs; mirror it for shorts.
Direction.The analysis rung has closed above a high. Longs only. Bearish rung: shorts only, or stand aside.
Liquidity and target.Mark what rests: equal lows, a range edge, a session low. Mark the target first — the nearest clear high — and check the room before anything else.
Sweep.Price trades through the level and closes back inside, wick or within two candles. Mark the extreme: that is the protected level and the stop goes beyond it.
Shift with imbalance.A candle close through the last lower high, leaving an imbalance. A wick is not a shift. A slow break with no gap is not a shift.
Zone and order.The last down candle before the shift leg is the zone. Limit at its top edge, stop beyond the protected level plus buffer, target at the marked liquidity. Under 1:2, no order.
Size, hold, record.Half to one percent. Alert set, hands off. Win or lose, the trade goes in the log with its screenshots.
The long version with drawings: zone model and sweep model. The morning version: notes.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: Where the leg began decides the target
entries.t:
Where the leg began decides the target
A rule earned in backtesting. Two sweeps can look identical on the entry timeframe and deserve completely different targets, because of what the higher timeframe is doing underneath.
| Setup | Gate | Target
| Sweep at a higher-TF zone, and the HTF leg itself started at a demand | With-trend bias | Far liquidity: the nearest HTF swing, else the week high or low
| Sweep at a higher-TF zone, but the HTF leg started at swept liquidity | With-trend bias | The next liquidity point on the entry TF only
| Bare sweep — no zone behind it | Only when the HTF itself shifted away from that swept liquidity | The next liquidity point on the entry TF only
| Bare sweep, HTF leg from a demand or from nothing | Refused. Label it, walk on. | —
The one-liner
A bare sweep trades only when the higher timeframe shifted from swept liquidity, and then it aims at the first pool in front of it — never at HTF highs or week lows. Far targets belong to zone-backed moves whose higher timeframe also came from a demand.
Exhibit A, drawn from a replay: BTCUSD 5m — sweep, MSS, and a target that stops at the first pool.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: Exhibit A: a replay, drawn
entries.t:
Exhibit A: a replay, drawn
BTCUSD 5m, replayed and marked by hand, then drawn here in the site’s style. Every mark is one of the key points above; the numbers are the replay’s.
Left to right: the 17:00 low rests at 66,365 (dotted, with the X where the 20:45 leg sweeps it); MSS at 66,785 when the 66,925 leg closes above it; that sweep creates the demand 66,310–66,365; the return taps it twice and the long fires from the second tap; the first bounce leaves $$$ at 66,435 and the 01:30 drop sweeps the 66,360 low (second X) before taking those $$$; each leg leaves a smaller zone and a higher protected low; the target stays 66,541.77 — the supply in front — while the 66,925 high above it is deliberately not the target.
The replay itself, frame by frame
Frame 1 — the sweep and the shift. X takes the 17:00 low at 66,365; the 22:40 leg closes above the 19:40 high (MSS, 66,785); the sweep creates the demand 66,310–66,365. The target is drawn before the entry: 66,541.77, the near edge of the supply in front. The 66,925 high is not the target.
Frame 2 — the fuel. The first bounce leaves $$$ at 66,435; the 01:30 drop sweeps the 66,360 low (second X), then takes those $$$ on the way up. A smaller zone and a higher protected low are left behind. Price stalls at about 66,520, short of target — nothing is chased.
Frame 3 — the staircase. Another swept low, another leg toward 66,541.77. Every rung ratchets the stop higher; the target does not move.
Frame 4 — the whole picture in one chart: sweep, MSS, sweep-created demand, internal fuel, ratcheting zones, and one target line from the first mark to the last.
What the replay teaches
The move fuels itself. Every leg up swept what the last leg left behind: the $$$ at 66,435, then the internal lows at 66,360. Untouched liquidity in front is fuel; spent liquidity behind is not a reason to re-enter.
The protected low ratchets. Each new internal sweep made a smaller zone and a higher protected low: 66,310, then 66,325, then 66,360. The stop moves up with them. The target never moves down to meet impatience.
A target not reached is not a reason to chase. Price stalled at about 66,520, eleven dollars short, twice. The staircase either continues from a new swept low or dies at the protected low. Adding at the stall is how a 4:1 becomes a 0:1.
Risk on the drawn trade: entry about 66,325, stop under 66,310, target 66,541.77 — roughly 4:1 before costs. The same maths the sequence demands.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: The skips are the strategy
entries.t:
The skips are the strategy
The entries take care of themselves once these are honest. Every line here has a losing trade behind it.
No sweep before the break — the break has no fuel and no protected level.
Break without imbalance — a slow drift through structure is not a shift.
Zone already tapped — a used zone is a story told twice.
Target already spent — if the liquidity you aim at was already taken, the move is gone. Ask: is my target still untouched?
Against the higher timeframe — except at a major level, with a nearer target and half the risk.
Protected level closed through — the idea is dead; delete the order, do not move the stop.
Under 1:2 — the maths does not pay for the misses.
High-impact news still being priced — that is a coin flip wearing a setup’s clothes.
What a skipped rule costsRun the live checklist

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: Timeframe pairs
entries.t:
Timeframe pairs
Analysis two rungs above the entry. The middle rung is optional; the pair is not.
| Analysis rung | Entry rung | Middle (optional)
| Weekly | 4H | Daily
| Daily | 1H | 4H
| 4H | 15m | 1H
| 1H | 5m | 15m
| 15m | 1m | 5m
If the entry rung gives no confirmation, the trade does not drop a rung — it waits. Full page: top-down analysis, the pair table.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: Two doors: 50 and 75
entries.t:
Two doors: 50 and 75
50% — equilibrium
This site’s line: buy below it, sell above it.
More trades, shallower entries, wider stops.
75% — the deep door
The posted rule: direction, sweep, BOS with imbalance, then a 75% retracement before the zone earns an order.
Fewer trades, deeper entries, tighter stops — and more moves that leave without you.
Not a contradiction: two doors into the same room. Pick one per setup type, write down which, and let the log decide after 50 samples — not after one missed move. See Note 11.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: Risk, in four lines
entries.t:
Risk, in four lines
Half to one percent of the account per idea. One idea, one risk.
Add only to a winner, only after a new sweep, shift and zone; move the first stop first; never more than the first size; same target; two adds maximum.
One re-entry after a stop-sweep, never a second.
Every trade recorded: screenshot, numbers, the rule that gave the entry, the rule that was bent.
The long form lives in the playbook risk rules and scaling & re-entry.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: “If it’s there, great. If not, I’ll wait.”
entries.t:
“If it’s there, great. If not, I’ll wait.”
4H for direction, liquidity sweep, BOS with imbalance, and a 75% retracement. If it’s there, great. If not, I’ll wait. A trade that never arrives costs nothing. A chased one costs R, and then it costs the next setup too, because you are in it when it comes.

entries.p: Key Points: The Whole Method in One Page
entries.h: Why there is no indicator for this
entries.t:
Why there is no indicator for this
It was tried
This method was once written as a chart indicator. The chart filled with lines, the structure still needed an eye, and the judgement — the part that decides — stayed exactly where it started: with you. So the code went and this page stayed. Mark it yourself, on your chart, in your own time. That is the point of the method.

entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Concept
Types of liquidity
Liquidity is where stop orders and breakout orders collect. They collect where many traders look at the same thing: a swing high, two lows at the same price, a line across the highs, the edge of a range, the high of the last session. Price often visits those places first and makes its lasting move afterwards. This page covers six such places, in two parts, and how to trade around them.
Concept, no pair named
Buy-side: stops above highs
Sell-side: stops below lows
From the post
“Many traders watch the same places. They use the same lines and take the same early entries. That is why price often goes to these places first, before it makes its real move.”
1.1 · Swing high & low
1.2 · Relative equal highs

How to read this page
The page follows two posts, “Types of Liquidity” Part 1 and Part 2. The slides give no pair, timeframe or price scale, and they draw no entries, stops or targets. $$$ marks resting liquidity. The order placement further down is my application of the site's playbook to these slides, not something the post shows.

entries.h: Liquidity at single levels: swings and equal highs and lows
entries.t:
Part 1
Liquidity at single levels: swings and equal highs and lows
The simplest liquidity sits at one price: above a high or below a low. The more times price has turned at that level, the more stops are stacked beyond it.

entries.h: Swing high and swing low
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. A rally makes a swing high and pulls back. Later a wick spikes above the swing high and price drops sharply, all the way to the swing low at the start of the rally, where a wick goes just below it.
Part 1, slide 1 — “The most obvious turning points on the chart. Stop losses gather above swing highs and below swing lows.”
1.1
Swing high and swing low
A swing high is a peak with lower candles on both sides. A swing low is the reverse. They are the first thing anyone marks on a chart, so they are where the most stops sit.
Above the swing high: buy stops from sellers, and buy orders from breakout traders.
Below the swing low: sell stops from buyers, and sell orders from breakout traders.
What price did: one wick went above the swing high and failed. Price then fell the whole way to the swing low and put a wick through that too.
One chart shows both jobs. The swing high was the liquidity that was taken before the move. The swing low was where the move went.
Rule from this slide
Mark the swing high and swing low of the leg you are trading. One of them is where a sweep can start a trade. The other is the target.

entries.h: Relative equal highs
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two highs, marked with arrows, turn at nearly the same level. A third push goes clearly above the line and price then falls back sharply.
Part 1, slide 2 — “Highs that are close, but not exactly equal. The third one goes above the line, then price comes back down.”
1.2
Relative equal highs
Two highs that turn at nearly the same price. They do not have to match to the pip. Traders see resistance and sell it, with stops just above.
The two touches: marked with arrows. Each one turned price down.
The third: price goes clearly above the line. The breakout does not hold.
Afterwards: large bearish candles bring price back under the line and well below it.
Just before the third push, a long wick dipped under the earlier lows and recovered. The slide does not label it. I read it as the sell-side being taken first, as on the trendline slides in Part 2.
Rule from this slide
After two touches of a level, do not sell the third touch with a stop just above. That stop is the liquidity. Wait for the push through and see whether it holds.

entries.h: Relative equal lows
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two lows, marked with arrows, turn at nearly the same level. A third dip goes below the line and price then climbs back above it and rallies.
Part 1, slide 3 — “Lows that are close, but not exactly equal. The third one goes below the line, then price comes back up.”
1.3
Relative equal lows
The mirror image. Two lows at nearly the same price look like support. Buyers enter there with stops just below.
The two touches: marked with arrows.
The third: a candle goes below the line. Its wick reaches further still.
Afterwards: price climbs back above the line and rallies to the dotted level above.
This is the pattern behind most of the long entries on this site: lows that look like support are taken, then price turns.

entries.h: Equal highs
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two highs at exactly the same level are marked with arrows. Price falls a long way, recovers in a V, pushes above the equal highs with wicks, and starts to come back under them.
Part 1, slide 4 — “Two highs at the same level. Then price goes above it, and comes back down.”
1.4
Equal highs
Two highs at exactly the same price. This is the cleanest version, often called a double top. The cleaner the level, the more traders use it, and the more stops sit above it.
The two highs: side by side at the left, marked with arrows.
The return: price falls a long way, then recovers the whole drop.
The take: wicks go above the level. The last candles are back under it.
The chart stops early
The slide says price “comes back down”. The chart ends only a little under the level, right after the take. The larger fall is not shown. At this point on a live chart you would not know yet whether it was a sweep or a pause before a breakout.

entries.h: Equal lows
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two lows at the same level are marked with arrows. Price rallies, tops out, then falls below the equal lows. The last candle is bullish and closes back up to a dotted level just above them.
Part 1, slide 5 — “Two lows at the same level. Then price goes below it, and comes back up.”
1.5
Equal lows
Two lows at the same price: a double bottom. Buyers treat it as strong support. Their stops sit just under it.
The two lows: at the left, marked with arrows. Price rallied a long way from the second.
The take: the rally rolls over and price falls through the level. It goes some distance below, with candle bodies under the line.
The return: one bullish candle closes back above the level, at the dotted line.
Price spent several candles below the level here. A sweep is not always a single wick. What counts is that price gets back above and then shifts structure.
Rule for all four equal-level slides
Equal and near-equal highs and lows are targets first. Price is drawn to them. They become entry areas only after they are taken and price has come back through.

entries.h: Liquidity has more than one job
entries.t:
Part 1, closing slide
Liquidity has more than one job
Chart: Text slide: Liquidity has more than one job. It is where price wants to go. It is fuel for big players to fill their orders. It can also be a target for your take profit.
Part 1, slide 6.
1 · A DESTINATION
“It is where price wants to go.”
Untouched highs and lows pull price toward them. Before a trade, ask which pool is nearest in each direction.
2 · FUEL
“It is fuel for big players to fill their orders.”
A large buyer needs sellers. Stops under a low are sell orders. Taking them lets the buyer fill, which is why reversals so often start with a sweep.
3 · A TARGET
“It can also be a target for your take profit.”
If price is drawn to a pool, that is where to exit. Place the take profit just before the level, not beyond it.

entries.h: Liquidity along lines and blocks of time: trendlines, ranges and sessions
entries.t:
Part 2
Liquidity along lines and blocks of time: trendlines, ranges and sessions
The same idea, spread over more than one price. Stops follow a diagonal line, sit on both sides of a range, or collect beyond the high and low of a session.

entries.h: Trendline liquidity above a downtrend
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. After a rally, price makes three lower highs joined by a dotted descending line marked with dollar signs. Price falls to a new low, then rallies through the line and above all the earlier highs before pulling back.
Part 2, slide 1 — “In a downtrend, sellers draw a line over the highs. They place their stops just above it. Price often breaks above the line first, takes those stops, then moves up.”
2.1
Trendline liquidity above a downtrend
Three lower highs line up. Anyone can join them with a line, and many do. They sell each touch and put the stop just above the line. Every touch adds more stops, so the liquidity above the line grows the longer the line holds.
What is above the line: buy stops from sellers, plus buy orders from traders waiting for a trendline break.
What price did: it rallied through the line and through every high behind it in one leg.
What came just before: a sharp drop to a new low under the earlier lows. The slide does not label it, but that drop took the sell-side first. The rally started from there.
Look at the last candles
After the break, price falls back a long way and the chart ends. The slide says price “moves up”, and it did go up through the line. Whether it kept going is not shown. Treat a trendline as a place price is drawn to, and take profit there. Do not assume the break continues.

entries.h: Trendline liquidity under an uptrend
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Price rises in steps. A dotted ascending line joins the lows, with dollar signs beneath it. At the top a long wick spikes above the highs, then large bearish candles fall through the line and continue far below it.
Part 2, slide 2 — “In an uptrend, buyers draw a line under the lows. They place their stops just below it. Price often breaks below the line first, takes those stops, then moves down.”
2.2
Trendline liquidity under an uptrend
The mirror image. Rising lows are joined by a line. Buyers buy each touch and place stops under it. Those stops are sell orders, and they sit in a neat diagonal row.
What is below the line: sell stops from buyers, plus sell orders from breakout traders.
What price did: large bearish candles cut through the line and kept falling, past the low the line started from.
What came just before: one long wick above the recent highs that closed back down. Again unlabelled, and again it is a sweep of the opposite side before the move.
What both trendline slides share
In both, price first takes liquidity on one side with a wick or a fast drop, then travels to the trendline liquidity on the other side. The trendline is the destination. The sweep on the opposite side is the place to look for the entry.

entries.h: Range liquidity
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Price moves sideways between a high and a low, each marked with a line and dollar signs. One large bullish candle breaks above the range high, the next candles reverse, fall through the range low and continue down.
Part 2, slide 3 — “In a range, stops sit outside both sides. Price often takes one side first, before it chooses a direction.”
2.3
Range liquidity
Price moves sideways between a high and a low. Traders who sell the top put stops above the high. Traders who buy the bottom put stops below the low. Breakout traders place orders at both. So a range has liquidity on each side.
The take: one large bullish candle closes above the range high. It looks like a breakout.
The failure: the next candles are bearish and bring price straight back inside the range.
The move: price falls through the whole range and through the low on the other side.
The breakout candle here closed above the high, not just a wick. That matters. A close beyond the level is not proof of a real break. What settles it is what the next few candles do.
Rule from this slide
Do not trade the first break of a range. Wait to see whether price holds outside it or comes back in. If it comes back in, the opposite side of the range becomes the target.

entries.h: Session highs and lows
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart with three shaded blocks. In the Asia block price falls, leaving an Asia high and an Asia low. In the London block price moves sideways, leaving a London high and a London low above the Asia low. In the New York block price first drops below the London low and the Asia low, then rallies above the London high and the Asia high to a New York high, and falls back.
Part 2, slide 4 — “Every session leaves a high and a low behind. Traders see them and place stops just beyond. A later session often runs through them first, then makes its real move.”
2.4
Session highs and lows
Each trading session is a block of time with its own high and low. Those levels are easy to see and easy to mark, so stops collect beyond them like any other high or low.
| Session | What it did on the slide | What it left
| Asia | Fell from the top of the chart | Asia high far above, Asia low below
| London | Moved sideways. Its low stayed above the Asia low | London high and London low, both inside the Asia range
| New York | Dropped first, through the London low and the Asia low. Then rallied through the London high and the Asia high | New York low and New York high
New York took the lows of both earlier sessions first. That drop was the visit to liquidity. The rally that followed was the larger move, and its targets were the London high and then the Asia high.
The slide also shows price falling back after the New York high. That high is now liquidity for the next session.
Session hours
The slide gives no clock times. As a rough guide in UTC: Asia about 00:00–09:00, London about 07:00–16:00, New York about 12:00–21:00. For Nairobi, add three hours. These shift by an hour with daylight saving in London and New York, and brokers define them differently. Check the session indicator on your own platform.

entries.h: What price does after it takes the liquidity
entries.t:
The other half
What price does after it takes the liquidity
Chart: Text slide: Some liquidity is easy to see. Some looks like a setup. Knowing where it is only gets you halfway. What price does after it takes it is the other half.
Part 2, slide 5 — the closing slide.
Marking liquidity tells you where price is likely to go. It does not tell you what happens when it arrives. There are two outcomes, and the candles after the take show which one you have.
| Check | Sweep (trade the reversal) | Real break (stand aside or trade with it)
| Where do the next candles close? | Back inside the level within a few candles | Outside it, candle after candle
| Does structure shift back? | Yes. A displacement candle breaks the last swing the other way (MSS) | No. Pullbacks stop at or beyond the old level
| What is left behind? | A fresh zone with an imbalance beside it, pointing back into the range | A fresh zone pointing in the direction of the break
| Does the higher timeframe agree? | The take ran into an HTF zone, or against the HTF trend | The take is in the direction of the HTF trend with room to run
The first three rows can be seen on the slides. The fourth is my addition and comes from the case studies, where each sweep happened at a higher-timeframe zone.
“Often” is not “always”
Every slide says price “often” takes the liquidity first. Real breakouts happen too, and from the level alone the two look identical. That is why the entry on this site comes after the shift and not at the level. A sell limit resting at a range high is a bet that the break fails, placed before there is any evidence.

entries.h: Entry, stop loss and take profit
entries.t:
Order placement
Entry, stop loss and take profit
For a short after buy-side liquidity is taken, as on the range slide. For a long after sell-side is taken, mirror every line. The slides draw no positions, so these placements follow the playbook used in the case studies.
Entry
Sell limit at the bottom edge of the supply zone left by the shift.
First price must take the high and come back under it.
Then a displacement candle must close below the last swing low (MSS), leaving an imbalance.
The supply zone is the last up candle, or small base, before that displacement. Rest the order at its near edge.
Stop loss
Above the sweep high, plus spread and a small buffer.
The sweep high is where the liquidity was taken. If price goes back above it, the break was real.
Not at the old range high or on the trendline. Those are the levels everyone else uses, which is why they were swept.
If that stop makes the trade smaller than 1:2 to the target, skip it.
Take profit
The untouched liquidity on the other side.
Swing or equal highs and lows: the level itself. Set the order just before it.
Range: the opposite side of the range.
Sessions: the nearest untaken session low, then the next one.
Trendline: the lows the line is drawn through. Take profit at the first one if a higher-timeframe demand zone sits in between.
Two uses for every level you mark
Liquidity that has just been taken and rejected gives the entry area. Liquidity that is still untouched in the direction of the trade gives the target. Before placing an order, name both. If you cannot name the liquidity that was taken, there is no entry. If you cannot name the liquidity ahead, there is no target.

entries.h: Step-by-step for each day
entries.t:
Repeatable strategy
Step-by-step for each day
A marking routine to run before the session you trade. It feeds the daily routine in the playbook.
Mark the swing high and swing low of the current leg.On the timeframe you take direction from, and one below it.
Mark equal and near-equal highs and lows.Two or more turns at about the same price. These hold the most stops.
Mark the previous sessions' highs and lows.Asia high and low before London. Asia and London highs and lows before New York. Add yesterday's high and low.
Mark any range.Three or more turns between the same high and low. Draw both sides.
Mark any trendline with three clean touches.Label it as liquidity. Do not buy or sell the touches.
Note which levels have already been taken.A taken level is finished. Only untouched levels are targets.
Check the higher-timeframe bias and zones.The strongest sweep takes liquidity on the side the bias is pushing away from, at an HTF zone. Example: a low taken inside HTF demand in an uptrend.
Wait for price to take a marked level.Set an alert at each level. Do nothing until one triggers.
Watch the next candles.Back inside and a shift with an imbalance: plan the trade. Holding outside: leave it alone.
Place the limit order at the zone the shift left.Stop beyond the sweep extreme. Target the nearest untouched level on the other side. At least 1:2, risk 0.5–1%.
Log it either way.Which type of liquidity, sweep or real break, and what price did afterwards.

entries.h: Where this has already appeared
entries.t:
In the case studies
Where this has already appeared
| Case | Type | What price did
| GBP/AUD long | Range liquidity | About nine hours of 15m range above the 1H demand. The range low was swept, then one candle shifted structure up
| BTC/USD long (1H) | Range liquidity | The lows of a 4H range were swept before the 4H shift, and the high above became the target
| USD/JPY long (1H) | Trendline liquidity | Rising 30m lows marked $$ sat above the 30m demand. Price later fell through them to reach the zone
| GBP/USD short | Trendline liquidity | Two rising lows joined by a $$$ line under the bounce. The short targeted the upper of the two
| BTC/USD long (1H) | Equal lows | Equal lows on the 1H were swept into demand, then the 1H shifted up
| GBP/JPY long | Equal or near-equal lows | A double low on the 15m was swept before the shift
| XAU/USD short | Swing high | The 4H took an old high, then shifted down
| XAU/USD long (5m) | Equal lows, then a swing high | The double bottom was underlined, swept by a wick, and the second MSS followed. The $$$ high above the zone was the target and was taken
| XAU/USD short (15m) | Swing highs (buy-side), twice | The retracement swept 3,906.5 then 3,899.8 before the shift down; the short then targeted the demand below instead of the highs
| XAU/USD short (4H→15m) | Swing high above, SSL pool below | The 15m swept its swing high under the 4H ceiling before shifting; the SSL lows below were the target and were broken
| The full sequence | Swing low and swing high | The swing low under the last BoS was swept for the entry. The high above (BSL) was the target
The first two used the range the same way as slide 3: one side taken first, the other side as the target. The USD/JPY case shows liquidity under a rising line being taken on the way to the zone. None of the case studies so far labels a session high or low. That type is untested on this site, so backtest it before giving it the same weight.
Related: inducement is the liquidity that forms after a shift, close to price. This page covers the liquidity that is already on the chart before the setup begins.
Keep this in proportion
The slides are examples picked because the liquidity was taken and price then moved. They do not say how often that happens. When you backtest, count three things for each marked level: taken and reversed, taken and continued, and never reached.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Strategy · Notes
Trading notes: the routine in order
The whole method as eleven short notes. Mark the trend. Check that the break had a sweep before it. Mark the protected low and the zone that caused the break. Wait for price to return, sweep and shift. Then place the order. It is written for longs; the table at the end mirrors it for shorts.
11 notes
Trend continuation
Same order every day
Short version
1 · Mark the trend
2 · Sweep before the break
3 · Mark the protected low
4 · Mark the demand that caused the break
5 · Mark the target
6 · Wait for price to return
7 · Inside the zone, wait for a sweep
8 · Wait for the shift
9 · Mark the small zone and place the order
10 · Hold, then record
11 · One setup, mastered
Shorts
How strict?

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: The short version
entries.t:
Read this every morning
The short version
Trend.Higher timeframe has closed above a high. I am looking for longs only.
Sweep before the break.The pullback before that break took a previous low. No sweep, no trade yet.
Protected low.The low of that sweep is marked. A close below it cancels the idea.
Demand.The last down candle before the break is marked. It is fresh, left an imbalance and is in discount.
Target.The weak high, or the supply in front of it. Room for 1:2 or more.
Wait.Alert at the zone. Nothing until it rings.
Sweep in the zone.Lower timeframe takes a small low and turns.
Shift.Lower timeframe closes above the last lower high, with an imbalance.
Order.Buy limit at the top of the small demand. Stop below the sweep low. Target from step 5. Risk 0.5–1%.
Hold and record.No changes. Screenshot and result in R.
One long from start to finish. The numbers match the notes below.
The idea in one sentence
The same three events happen twice: sweep, break, zone on the higher timeframe to give you the place, then sweep, shift, zone on the lower timeframe to give you the entry.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Mark the trend
entries.t:
Note 1 · Higher timeframe
Mark the trend
Open the higher timeframe and decide whether it is making higher highs and higher lows, or lower lows and lower highs.
Do this
Find the last break of structure: a candle close above the previous high (uptrend) or below the previous low (downtrend).
Write one word: long or short. You only trade in that direction.
Mark the high that the break made. It is the weak high.
Stop here if
Price is moving sideways and has not broken a high or low recently.
The last two breaks point in opposite directions.
Why
Trading with the higher timeframe means the larger orders are on your side. Every case study on this site starts here.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Check the break: was there a sweep first?
entries.t:
Note 2 · Higher timeframe
Check the break: was there a sweep first?
In a continuing uptrend, the pullback before the break must have gone below a previous low and taken the stops there. Only then did price break the high.
Do this
Look at the pullback that came before the break of the high.
Find the low it took: a previous swing low, equal lows, or the low of a range.
Confirm price went below that low and then turned up. That is the sweep.
Note which low it was. An internal low is the minimum. A dip under the previous external low that closed back above is stronger. See internal and external structure.
If you find it, the break is a good one. Carry on.
Stop here if
The high broke without the pullback taking any low. Treat the low as unprotected and wait: price may return to sweep it. That sweep can become your setup.
The break was a wick only, with no candle close beyond the high.
Why
A sweep collects the sell stops resting under the low. Those stops become the buy orders that fuel the break. When a high breaks with no sweep before it, the stops under the low are still there, and price often comes back for them before the trend continues. See a good break of structure.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Mark the protected low
entries.t:
Note 3 · Higher timeframe
Mark the protected low
The low of the pullback that swept and then broke the high is now the protected low. The trend is intact while price stays above it.
Do this
Draw a line at the lowest point of the sweep.
Label it “protected low”.
Remember what it means: a candle close below it cancels the long idea.
Stop here if
A candle has already closed below this low. The trend has changed; go back to note 1.
Why
This low did its job: it took liquidity and produced a break. Price has no reason to return below it while the trend holds. That makes it the level your stop loss hides behind, and the level that tells you when you are wrong.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Mark the demand that caused the break
entries.t:
Note 4 · Higher timeframe
Mark the demand that caused the break
The zone is the last down candle before the move that broke the high. It sits at or just above the protected low.
Do this
Draw the zone from that candle’s low to its high.
Check it left an imbalance: a fast move away with a gap between candles.
Check it is fresh: price has not come back to it since.
Check it is in discount: in the lower half of the move from the protected low to the new high.
Stop here if
The zone has already been tapped.
There is no clear candle, or the move away was slow and overlapping.
The zone is in the upper half of the move (premium).
Why
This is where the buying that broke the high began. Orders that were not filled on the way up are still waiting there. A zone that did not break structure has not shown that strength. See supply and demand.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Mark the target
entries.t:
Note 5 · Higher timeframe
Mark the target
Decide where the trade ends before you look for an entry.
Do this
Mark the weak high from note 1. Price is expected to break it.
If a supply zone sits in front of that high, the target is the lower edge of that zone instead.
Measure from the demand zone to the target. You need room for at least 1:2.
Stop here if
The target is too close for 1:2.
Why
The target comes from the chart, not from the reward you would like. If the room is not there, the trade is not there.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Wait for price to return
entries.t:
Note 6 · Waiting
Wait for price to return
Set an alert at the top of the demand zone and close the chart.
Do this
Set the alert.
Do nothing until it rings. No trades in the middle of the move.
Stop here if
Price reaches the target before it returns to the zone. Delete the zone and start again.
Why
Most losing trades are taken between the zones out of boredom. The alert does the watching for you.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Inside the zone, wait for a sweep
entries.t:
Note 7 · Lower timeframe
Inside the zone, wait for a sweep
When the alert rings, drop to the lower timeframe. Price should take one more small low inside or just into the zone.
Do this
Watch price arrive in the zone.
Wait for it to go below a lower-timeframe low and turn back up.
This is an internal sweep: the protected low from note 3 must still be intact.
Mark the low of that sweep. Your stop will go below it.
Stop here if
A candle closes below the higher-timeframe zone. The zone has failed.
Price drops through the zone without slowing.
Why
This is the same event as note 2 on a smaller scale. It shows the selling is being absorbed at your zone, and it gives you a tight, logical place for the stop.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Wait for the shift
entries.t:
Note 8 · Lower timeframe
Wait for the shift
After the sweep, a lower-timeframe candle must close above the last lower high. That is the shift (also called MSS or CHoCH).
Do this
Mark the last lower high before the sweep.
Wait for a candle to close above it.
Check the move left an imbalance.
Stop here if
Price only wicks above the high and closes back below.
The shift is slow and leaves no imbalance.
Why
The shift is the confirmation. Before it, price touching the zone is only a touch. After it, the lower timeframe has turned in the direction of the higher one.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Mark the small zone and place the order
entries.t:
Note 9 · Lower timeframe
Mark the small zone and place the order
The entry zone is the last down candle before the shift move. This is the same rule as note 4, one timeframe down.
Do this
Draw the small demand zone.
Buy limit at its top edge.
Stop loss below the sweep low from note 7, plus 5–10 pips and the spread.
Take profit at the target from note 5.
Check the reward is at least 1:2. Risk 0.5–1% of the account.
Stop here if
Reward is below 1:2.
Price reaches the target before filling the order. Cancel it.
Why
Entering on the return to the small zone gives a better price and a smaller stop than buying the shift candle. If price leaves without filling you, you have lost nothing.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Hold, then record
entries.t:
Note 10 · After the order
Hold, then record
Once the order is placed, the work is done.
Do this
Leave the stop and target where they are.
When the trade closes, save a screenshot and write the result in R.
Review every 20 trades, not every trade.
Stop here if
You feel like moving the stop to break-even early. The plan already has a stop.
Why
One trade proves nothing. Twenty trades taken the same way show whether the routine works for you.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: Catch one move, not every move
entries.t:
Note 11 · Before everything else
Catch one move, not every move
A posted caption worth reading every morning, kept here word for word:
“You don’t have to catch every move. Seriously, stop feeling like you’re missing out every time price moves without you. I used to think the more opportunities I found, the better trader I’d become. But think about it. Wouldn’t you rather master one setup than spend your whole life chasing ten different ones? That’s what I focus on now. 4H for direction, liquidity sweep, BOS with imbalance, and a 75% retracement. If it’s there, great. If not, I’ll wait. And trust me, you’ll be surprised how much easier trading feels when you stop trying to catch everything.”
— posted caption, added to this page at the site owner’s request
The four conditions, in this site’s words
4H for direction — the analysis rung of the pair table. One word: long or short.
Liquidity sweep — notes 2 and 7: something resting must be taken first.
BOS with imbalance — note 8: the shift, with its FVG beside it.
75% retracement — the entry filter: price must give back three quarters of the leg before the zone earns an order.
Where 75% differs from this site
This site’s line is 50%: equilibrium, buy below, sell above. The caption’s 75% is a deeper door.
Deeper means fewer trades, deeper entries, tighter stops — and more moves that leave without you.
Not a contradiction: a stricter door on the same room. Test both in the log and keep the one your numbers support.
“If not, I’ll wait”
That clause is the whole checklist in four words. A trade that never arrives costs nothing; a chased one costs R. The feeling of missing out is not a signal — why a trade failed is what chasing leaves behind.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: The same notes for shorts
entries.t:
The same notes for shorts
| Note | Long | Short
| 1 Trend | Close above a high | Close below a low
| 2 Sweep before the break | Pullback took a previous low | Pullback took a previous high
| 3 Protected point | Protected low | Protected high
| 4 Zone | Demand: last down candle before the break, in discount | Supply: last up candle before the break, in premium
| 5 Target | Weak high, or supply in front of it | Weak low, or demand in front of it
| 7 Sweep in the zone | Small low taken | Small high taken
| 8 Shift | Close above the last lower high | Close below the last higher low
| 9 Order | Buy limit at the top edge; stop below the sweep low | Sell limit at the bottom edge; stop above the sweep high plus spread
The short, drawn step by step
The same drawings as the long notes, turned upside down: a fall instead of a rally, a supply instead of a demand, the stop above and the target below. The black dot is where price is at that note. Notes 6 and 10 add no new mark, so they keep no drawing: wait, then leave it alone.
Note 1 — a candle close below the last low. The trend is down; longs are off the board.
Note 2 — the pullback took a previous high first ($$$, X). No sweep before the break, no trade.
Note 3 — the sweep high is the protected high. A close above it cancels the idea.
Note 4 — the supply: last up candles before the break, in premium. Sell only above the 50% line.
Note 5 — the target: the weak low the break left, or a demand zone in front of it. Room for 1:2 or nothing.
Note 7 — inside the zone, the small highs are swept (X). That sweep is the fuel for the fall.
Note 8 — the shift: a close below the last higher low, with an imbalance. Only now does the zone earn an order.
Note 9 — sell limit at the bottom edge, stop above the sweep high plus spread, target at the weak low. Then wait.

entries.p: Trading Notes: The Routine in Order
entries.h: How strict is “must”?
entries.t:
How strict is “must”?
The sweep before the break is a filter you choose to apply, not a law of the market. Highs do break without a sweep and price sometimes keeps going. The filter is worth keeping because it removes the breaks that are most likely to be pulled back, and because it gives you a clear protected low for the stop.
Keep it as a fixed rule while you backtest. A rule you bend cannot be measured.
Count the setups you skipped because of it. If many of them would have won, review the rule after 50 samples, not after one.
When a low was not swept, mark it as liquidity. A later sweep of that low followed by a shift is a setup for the sweep model.
